senses.definition: A senior person putting their own standing behind a person or a piece of work.
senses.caution: The line that matters: a mentor talks to you, a sponsor talks about you. Describing someone as your sponsor when all they have given is advice overstates what you have, and it is embarrassing when the room knows them better than you do. The word also means paid branding, so with a mixed audience say executive sponsor the first time and let the rest run short.
senses.example: The programme has funding and it has sponsorship, so when finance pushed back last week it was not my fight alone.

cues.text: A director asks what the failed initiative was really missing, and the honest answer is that nobody senior owned it once it got hard.
You are advising a colleague who has no shortage of mentors and keeps being passed over, and you want the word for the thing mentoring is not.
Before starting a programme that cuts across three teams, you want one word for the senior commitment you will ask for beyond the budget.
A friend's daughter is trying to break into an industry where advice is easy to come by and an opened door is not.
At a climbing club an experienced member vouches for a newcomer and puts her own standing behind them.

distractors: Advice given privately to someone earlier in their career.
The budget line that pays for a programme's staff and tools.
A written record of who is accountable for each deliverable in a plan.
The practice of pairing a new joiner with a colleague who answers their questions.
A senior person's public disagreement with a decision their own leadership has taken.
